81--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
82---     `INCOMING BOCHUM MATERIAL summarized by Claude (old/bochum-lf-updates/AltAuto.v): the
83---        Bochum LF updates extend AltAuto's discussion of the sequencing
84---        tactical with new material on Rocq's "local form with `..`":
85---
86---          T; [T1 .. | Tn]
87---
88---        which applies T1 to the first goal, Tn to the last, and T1 to all
89---        goals in between (variants: T; [T1 | .. | Tn] applies nothing in
90---        between; the `..` may also appear first, last, or alone).  The new
91---        material illustrates this by revisiting star_app from IndProp:
92---
93---          Lemma star_app'': forall T (s1 s2 : list T) (re : reg_exp T),
94---            s1 =~ Star re ->
95---            s2 =~ Star re ->
96---            s1 ++ s2 =~ Star re.
97---          Proof.
98---            intros T s1 s2 re H1.
99---            remember (Star re) as re' eqn:Eq.
100---            induction H1
101---              as [|x'|s1 re1 s2' re2 Hmatch1 IH1 Hmatch2 IH2
102---                  |s1 re1 re2 Hmatch IH|re1 s2' re2 Hmatch IH
103---                  |re''|s1 s2' re'' Hmatch1 IH1 Hmatch2 IH2];
104---              [discriminate .. | intros H; apply H | idtac]. (* <=== *)
105---            (* MStarApp *)
106---            intros H1. rewrite <- app_assoc.
107---            apply MStarApp.
108---            + apply Hmatch1.
109---            + apply IH2.
110---              * apply Eq.
111---              * apply H1.
112---          Qed.
113---
114---        (first shown in its long form with all seven cases spelled out, then
115---        shortened as above).  Bochum also adds a QUIETSOLUTION alternate
116---        solution to AltAuto's re_opt exercise that uses nested `..` lists
117---        instead of `try`, and rewords the introduction of `T; T'` to say
118---        simply that it is "equivalent to locally performing T' on all the
119---        subgoals".
120---
121---        To incorporate: Lean has no direct analogue of the positional
122---        `[T1 .. | Tn]` goal-selector list; the closest idioms are
123---        case-labelled alternatives (`case ... =>`/`next`), `all_goals`,
124---        and `first`.  A future pass should decide whether to add a
125---        parallel discussion here (e.g. using `star_app` below, proving the
126---        six non-MStarApp cases uniformly) or to record the Rocq material
127---        as intentionally unported.`

339+--  Note that this definition is *polymorphic*: Regular

344+--  We connect regular expressions and strings by defining
345+--  when a regular expression *matches* some string.
346+
347+--  Informally this looks as follows:
348+
349+--  - The regular expression `EmptySet` does not match any
350+--    string.
351+
352+--  - `EmptyStr` matches the empty string `[]`.
353+
354+--  - `Char x` matches the one-character string `x`.
355+
356+--  - If `re₁` matches `s₁`, and `re₂` matches `s₂`, then
357+--    `App re₁ re₂` matches `s₁ ++ s₂`.
358+
359+--  - If at least one of `re₁` and `re₂` matches `s`, then
360+--    `Union re₁ re₂` matches `s`.
361+
362+--  - Finally, if we can write some string `s` as the
363+--    concatenation of a sequence of strings
364+--    `s = s₁ ++ ... ++ sₖ`, and the expression `re` matches
365+--    each one of the strings `sᵢ`, then `Star re` matches
366+--    `s`.
367+
368+--    In particular, the sequence of strings may be empty,
369+--    so `Star re` always matches the empty string `[]` no
370+--    matter what `re` is.
371+
372+--  We can easily translate this intuition into a set of
373+--  rules, where we write `s =~ re` to say that `re` matches
374+--  `s`:
375+
376+--    ─────────────── (mEmpty)
377+--    [] =~ EmptyStr
378+
379+--    ─────────────── (mChar)
380+--    [x] =~ (Char x)
381+
382+--    s₁ =~ re₁     s₂ =~ re₂
383+--    ─────────────────────────── (mApp)
384+--    (s₁ ++ s₂) =~ (App re₁ re₂)
385+
386+--    s₁ =~ re₁
387+--    ───────────────────── (mUnionL)
388+--    s₁ =~ (Union re₁ re₂)
389+
390+--    s₂ =~ re₂
391+--    ───────────────────── (mUnionR)
392+--    s₂ =~ (Union re₁ re₂)
393+
394+--    ──────────────── (mStar0)
395+--    [] =~ (Star re)
396+
397+--    s₁ =~ re     s₂ =~ (Star re)
398+--    ──────────────────────────── (mStarApp)
399+--    (s₁ ++ s₂) =~ (Star re)
400+
401+--  This directly corresponds to the following inductive
402+--  definition:

712--- ### The "Weak" Pumping Lemma
713-
714--- One of the first really interesting theorems in the theory
715--- of regular expressions is the so-called *pumping lemma*,
716--- which states, informally, that any sufficiently long string
717--- `s` matching a regular expression `re` can be "pumped" by
718--- repeating some middle section of `s` an arbitrary number of
719--- times to produce a new string also matching `re`. For the
720--- sake of simplicity, this exercise considers a slightly
721--- weaker theorem than is usually stated in courses on automata
722--- theory ─ hence the name `weak_pumping`. The stronger one can
723--- be found below.
724-
725--- To get started, we need to define "sufficiently long." Since
726--- we are working in a constructive logic, we actually need to
727--- be able to *calculate*, for each regular expression `re`, a
728--- minimum length for strings `s` to guarantee "pumpability."
657+--  ### The "Weak" Pumping Lemma
658+

663+--  be "pumped" by repeating some middle section of `s` an

666+--  considers a slightly weaker theorem than is usually
667+--  stated in courses on automata theory ─ hence the name

794--- The (weak) pumping lemma itself says that, if `s =~ re` and
795--- if the length of `s` is at least the pumping constant of
796--- `re`, then `s` can be split into three substrings
797--- `s₁ ++ s₂ ++ s₃` in such a way that `s₂` can be repeated any
798--- number of times and the result, when combined with `s₁` and
799--- `s₃`, will still match `re`. Since `s₂` is also guaranteed
800--- not to be the empty string, this gives us a (constructive!)
801--- way to generate strings matching `re` that are as long as we
802--- like.
803-

806--- assemble to prove the main lemma.

119--- Lean has a very flexible notation system. Operators like
120--- `||` and `&&` are defined with specified precedence and
121--- associativity. For example, the `infixl` directive above
122--- states that `&&` is an infix operator, has precedence 35,
123--- and is left-associative, while `||` is also infix and
124--- left-associative and has precedence 30. This means that
125--- `MyBool.true || MyBool.false && MyBool.false` is parsed as
126--- `MyBool.true || (MyBool.false && MyBool.false)`.
127-

1079--- ### Exercise (3 stars): binary ⭐⭐⭐

1081--- We can generalize our unary representation of natural
1082--- numbers to the more efficient binary representation by
1083--- treating a binary number as a sequence of constructors `b0`
1084--- and `b1` (representing 0s and 1s), terminated by a `z`.
1085-
1086--- For example:
1087-
1088--- decimal                binary   unary
1089---       0                     z   zero
1090---       1                  b1 z   succ zero
1091---       2             b0 (b1 z)   succ (succ zero)
1092---       3             b1 (b1 z)   succ (succ (succ zero))
1093---       4        b0 (b0 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))
1094---       5        b1 (b0 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))
1095---       6        b0 (b1 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))
1096---       7        b1 (b1 (b1 z))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero))))))
1097---       8   b0 (b0 (b0 (b1 z)))   succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ (succ zero)))))))
1098-
1099--- Note that the low-order bit is on the left and the
1100--- high-order bit is on the right — the opposite of the way
1101--- binary numbers are usually written. This choice makes them
1102--- easier to manipulate.
1103-
1104--- (Comprehension check: What unary numeral does `b0 z`
1105--- represent?)

258+    | stx => throwErrorAt stx "Could not parse inversion alternatives"

8--- Note to developers:
9---     `HIDE: BCP 25: After teaching the chapter this semester, I feel
10---     that (a) the Ev example, while arguably suboptimal, actually works
11---     acceptably well. (I just wish that the n in ``ev_succ_succ` n H` was not
12---     two smaller than the n that is being shown to be even — that's
13---     always awkward.  Wonder if there is some clever way around that...)
14---
15---     However, (b) the chapter is very long, and quite a few of the
16---     exercises are hard, especially if you do as I did this year and
17---     require the advanced exercises for everybody (on the assumption
18---     that they could get plenty of help from LLMs, etc.).  I think it
19---     really needs to be at least significantly trimmed, if not split up.`
20---
21---     `HIDE: MRC 3/22: I offer a few remarks. I'm putting them here, above
22---     the BCP'21 comment, not to say that they are in any way more
23---     important; rather, just to preserve some chronological legibility.
24---
25---     - This chapter is an outlier in length. It now has the maximum line
26---       length (in the FULL version) of any chapter in LF, at about 2300
27---       LoC. That's a z-score of about 1.75 for the "blue arrow" chapters
28---       in the dependency diagram.
29---
30---     - This chapter has 39 exercises, of which 25 (!) are optional.
31---
32---     - The running example of evenness is known to be uncompelling
33---       because it is representable without inductively-defined
34---       propositions. There do exist compelling examples:
35---
36---       + Functions like `factorial` whose "natural" definitions are not
37---         structurally recursive. [Coq'Art 8.4]  [BCP 25: FWIW, I don't
38---         find the "natural" definition of factorial suitable for present
39---         purposes: the reasons it is better and more natural than a
40---         simple fixpoint seem rather subtle.]
41---
42---       + Partial functions.
43---
44---       + Relations (that are not strictly functions).
45---
46---     I have a couple of personal opinions based on those observations:
47---
48---     - I favor BCP'21's "path 1" of de-emphasizing (to the extent
49---       perhaps of eliminating) evenness.
50---
51---     - I favor re-factoring this chapter into two files, with a main
52---       (blue) path that covers the essentials without cluttering
53---       optional exercises throughout the file.`

55---     HIDE: BCP '21: This chapter has been the subject of a
56---     lot of discussion over the past couple of years, with
57---     lots of people expressing dissatisfaction with the use
58---     of evenness as a main example. In this revision, I have
59---     attempted a compromise: keeping evenness as the running
60---     example (because, aside from the artificiality of the
61---     example, it is pretty well polished) but preceding it
62---     with short discussions of several better-motivated
63---     examples.
64---
65---     I'm not yet convinced that this goes far enough, though
66---     (I was not satisfied with my lecture on this part of the
67---     chapter, even after adding these examples, though I did
68---     do some further streamlining afterward and there are
69---     some further opportunities for streamlining — perhaps
70---     enough to make the present treatment palatible). I see
71---     three possible paths forward:
72---
73---     - 1. Choose a better example and simply replace all the even
74---          stuff. (But which one is better? I don't think we've
75---          found it yet.)
76---
77---     - 2. Mix and match ─ use different examples from the top of
78---          the chapter to make different points.
79---
80---     - 3. Leave the examples as-is but streamline as much as
81---          possible so we don't get stuck in them.
82---
83---     Here, for reference, is the whole discussion from
84---     before:
85---
86---     -----------------
87---
88---     CH: In my Lyon course it became obvious to pretty much
89---     everyone that the inductive definition of evenness that
90---     this chapter uses intensiviely is so silly and
91---     artificial that it makes understanding very hard for
92---     most students. There's zero need to define evenness
93---     inductively, when `∃ k, n = 2*k` does the job fine, so
94---     inductive propositions seem to students not something
95---     useful, but just self-inflicted pain. All the inductive
96---     propositions, up to subsequences and the matching on
97---     Regular Expressions at the end, have this useless
98---     self-inflicted pain flavour. So I returned to this the
99---     following morning and showed to the students how to
100---     define reflexive-transitive closure as an inductive
101---     relation, and afterwards the were able to follow much
102---     better. The code I quickly hacked up for this is at:
103---     https://prosecco.gforge.inria.fr/personal/hritcu/teaching/lyon2019/Multi.v
104---
105---     BCP: Yes, this chapter needs a revamp! For the moment I
106---     am going to just add a couple of sentences to the
107---     opening sequence below, to warn students about this
108---     potential confusion. Moving forward, I wonder whether
109---     something like ordered binary trees would be a simple
110---     enough running example.
111---
112---     BCP 20: I remain puzzled by what is the really right
113---     example for this chapter. Ordered trees (and sorted
114---     lists) don't feel quite right because students might
115---     think we should define them with Fixpoint, not
116---     inductive. APT 21: Ordered trees are also surprisingly
117---     complex to describe (see VFA/SearchTree.v). Maybe
118---     Permutations would be be a good choice? The only problem
119---     is convincing students that the standard Lean inductive
120---     definition is actually correct (see VFA/Perm.v)!
121---
122---     We should also think about how to make the material flow
123---     better between this chapter and ProofObjects. When
124---     lecturing about this one I ended up introducing a lot of
125---     the concepts from that one.
126---
127---     --------
128---
129---     LATER: BCP 19: After lecturing on the first part of this
130---     chapter, I'm afraid I have to agree that the Ev / even /
131---     evenb stuff is a total mess. Besides the "why are there
132---     so many definitions of evenness?" problem, evenness is
133---     just not a very natural inductively defined proposition
134---     as a first example, because we already have so many
135---     intuitions about what evenness is, and they clash with
136---     the new definition.
137---
138---     So what to do?
139---
140---     An early version of this chapter, years ago, used a
141---     completely artificial inductively defined property of
142---     numbers (0 is beautiful, twice a beautiful number is
143---     beautiful, etc.). We could consider going back to that.
144---     Or perhaps there is a more natural example, either
145---     involving numbers or perhaps using some other inductive
146---     structure like lists or binary trees. Not sure what's
147---     best.
148---
149---     A related issue is that later chapters (ProofObjects,
150---     IndPrinciples) also rely heavily on this example. Sigh.
151---

153---     the propositional definition from `Ev` to `eveni`, for
154---     symmetry with `evenb`, and renaming the definition that
155---     says "a number is even if it is twice something" to
156---     `evend`. What do people think of this?
157---

166--- ## Inductively Defined Propositions
167-
168--- In the Logic chapter, we looked at several ways of writing
169--- propositions, including conjunction, disjunction, and
170--- existential quantification.
171-
172--- In this chapter, we bring yet another new tool into the mix:
173--- *inductively defined propositions*.
174-
175--- To begin, some examples...
176-
177--- ### Example: The Collatz Conjecture
178-
179--- The *Collatz Conjecture* is a famous open problem in number
180--- theory.
181-
182--- Its statement is quite simple. First, we define a function
183--- `csf` on numbers, as follows (where `csf` stands for
184--- "Collatz step function"):
6+--  # IndProp: Inductively Defined Propositions
7+
8+--  ## Inductively Defined Propositions
9+
10+--  In the Logic chapter, we looked at several ways of
11+--  writing propositions, including conjunction,
12+--  disjunction, and existential quantification.
13+
14+--  In this chapter, we bring yet another new tool into the
15+--  mix: *inductively defined propositions*.
16+
17+--  To begin, some examples...
18+
19+--  ### Example: The Collatz Conjecture
20+
21+--  The *Collatz Conjecture* is a famous open problem in
22+--  number theory.
23+
24+--  Its statement is quite simple. First, we define a
25+--  function `csf` on numbers, as follows (where `csf`
26+--  stands for "Collatz step function"):
18527 
18628 def div2 (n : Nat) : Nat :=
18729   match n with
19335   if n.even then div2 n
19436   else (3 * n) + 1
19537 
196--- Next, we look at what happens when we repeatedly apply `csf`
197--- to some given starting number. For example, `csf 12` is `6`,
198--- and `csf 6` is `3`, so by repeatedly applying `csf` we get
199--- the sequence `12, 6, 3, 10, 5, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1`.
200-
201--- Similarly, if we start with `19`, we get the longer sequence
202--- `19,
203--- 58, 29, 88, 44, 22, 11, 34, 17, 52, 26, 13, 40, 20, 10, 5, 16, 8,
204--- 4, 2, 1`.
205-
206--- Both of these sequences eventually reach `1`. The question
207--- posed by Collatz was: Is the sequence starting from *any*
208--- positive natural number guaranteed to reach `1` eventually?
209-
210--- To formalize this question in Lean, we might try to define a
211--- recursive *function* that calculates the total number of
212--- steps that it takes for such a sequence to reach `1`. You
213--- can write this definition in a standard programming
214--- language, but it is rejected by Lean's termination checker,
215--- since the argument to the recursive call, `csf n`, is not
216--- "obviously smaller" than `n`.

335181 inductive CollatzHoldsFor : Nat → Prop where
336182   | chf_one  : CollatzHoldsFor 1
339185   | chf_odd  {n : Nat} (h₁ : n.even = false)

385--- ### Example: Binary Relation for Comparing Numbers
386-
387--- A binary *relation* on a set `α` has Lean type
388--- `α → α → Prop`. This is a family of propositions
389--- parameterized by two elements of `α` ─ i.e., a proposition
390--- about pairs of elements of `α`.
391-
392--- For example, one familiar binary relation on `Nat` is
393--- `Le : Nat → Nat → Prop`, the less-than-or-equal-to relation,
394--- which can be inductively defined by the following two rules:
395-
396---     ─────── (le_refl)
397---     Le n n
398-
399---     Le n m
400---   ──────────── (le_step)
401---   Le n (m + 1)

214+--  bright future as a number theorist! But don't spend too
215+--  long on it ─ it's been open since 1937.

416--- ### Example: Transitive Closure
417-
418--- Another example: The *transitive closure* of a relation `R`
419--- is the smallest relation that contains `R` and that is
420--- transitive. This can be defined by the following two rules:
421-
422---                 R x y
423---            ─────────────── (t_step)
424---            ClosTrans R x y
425-
426---   ClosTrans R x y    ClosTrans R y z
427---   ──────────────────────────────────── (t_trans)
428---            ClosTrans R x z
429-
430--- In Lean this looks as follows:
249+--  ### Example: Transitive Closure
250+
251+--  Another example: The *transitive closure* of a relation
252+--  `R` is the smallest relation that contains `R` and that
253+--  is transitive. This can be defined by the following two
254+--  rules:
255+
256+--                  R x y

390+--  ### Example: Evenness (yet again)
391+
392+--  We've already seen two ways of stating a proposition
393+--  that a number `n` is even: We can say
394+
395+--  (1) `Nat.even n = true` (using the recursive boolean
396+--  function `Nat.even`), or

399+--  quantifier).
400+
401+--  A third possibility, which we'll use as a simple running
402+--  example in this chapter, is to say that a number is even
403+--  if we can *establish* its evenness from the following
404+--  two rules:

689--- ## Using Evidence in Proofs
690-
691--- Besides *constructing* evidence that numbers are even, we
692--- can also *destruct* such evidence, reasoning about how it
693--- could have been built.
694-
695--- Defining `Ev` with an `inductive` declaration tells Lean not
696--- only that the constructors `Ev.ev_0` and `Ev.ev_succ_succ`
697--- are valid ways to build evidence that some number is `Ev`,
698--- but also that these two constructors are the *only* ways to
699--- build evidence that numbers are `Ev`.
700-
701--- In other words, if someone gives us evidence `e` for the
702--- proposition `Ev n`, then we know that `e` must be one of two
703--- things:
704-
705--- - `e = ev_0` and `n = 0`, or
706-
707--- - `e = ev_succ_succ n' e'` and `n = n' + 2`, where `e'` is
708---   evidence for `Ev n'`.
709-
710--- This suggests that it should be possible to do *case
711--- analysis* and even *induction* on evidence of evenness...
712-
713--- ### Destructing and Inverting Evidence
714-
715--- We can prove our characterization of evidence for `Ev n`,
716--- using `cases`.
521+--  ## Using Evidence in Proofs
522+
523+--  Besides *constructing* evidence that numbers are even,
524+--  we can also *destruct* such evidence, reasoning about
525+--  how it could have been built.
526+
527+--  Defining `Ev` with an `inductive` declaration tells Lean
528+--  not only that the constructors `Ev.ev_0` and
529+--  `Ev.ev_succ_succ` are valid ways to build evidence that
530+--  some number is `Ev`, but also that these two
531+--  constructors are the *only* ways to build evidence that
532+--  numbers are `Ev`.
533+
534+--  In other words, if someone gives us evidence `e` for the
535+--  proposition `Ev n`, then we know that `e` must be one of
536+--  two things:
537+
538+--  - `e = ev_0` and `n = 0`, or
539+
540+--  - `e = ev_succ_succ n' e'` and `n = n' + 2`, where `e'`
541+--    is evidence for `Ev n'`.
542+
543+--  This suggests that it should be possible to do *case
544+--  analysis* and even *induction* on evidence of
545+--  evenness...
546+
547+--  ### Destructing and Inverting Evidence
548+
549+--  We can prove our characterization of evidence for
550+--  `Ev n`, using `cases`.
717551 
718552 theorem ev_inversion (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) :
719553     (n = 0) ∨ ∃ n', n = n' + 2 ∧ Ev n' := by
721555   | ev_0 => left; rfl
722556   | @ev_succ_succ n h => right; exists n
723557 
724--- Facts like this are often called "inversion lemmas" because
725--- they allow us to "invert" some given information to reason
726--- about all the different ways it could have been derived.
727-

733-

735--- `contradiction` (D) these tactics are not sufficient to
736--- solve the goal.

739--- structure proofs:

571+--  solve the goal.
572+

574+--  help structure proofs:

741576 theorem ev_succ_succ_ev (n : Nat) (h : Ev (n + 2)) : Ev n := by
742577   apply ev_inversion at h
745580   subst heq
746581   exact h₂
747582

666+--  ### Induction on Evidence
667+
668+--  If this story feels familiar, it is no coincidence: We
669+--  encountered similar problems in the Induction chapter,
670+--  when trying to use case analysis to prove results that
671+--  required induction. And once again the solution is...
672+--  induction!
673+
674+--  Let's try proving that lemma again:
864675 
865676 theorem Nat.ev_Even (n : Nat) (h : Ev n) : Even n := by
866677   induction h with
871682     let ⟨k, hk⟩ := ih
872683     exists k + 1; rw [double_succ, hk]
873684

226--- ### Tip: the `rw` tactic
227-
228--- As you've probably noticed, a common pattern in Lean proofs
229--- is `rewrite [...]` followed by `rfl`. There is a tactic that
230--- combines these two steps: `rw [...]` will automatically
231--- close the goal if the rewrite makes the goal true by
232--- definition. For example, instead of writing
233-
234---   rewrite [double_zero]; rfl
235-
236--- We could write this:
237-
238---   rw [double_zero]
239-
240--- If `rw` leaves a goal that looks definitionally true, try
241--- adding `rfl` after it.

412--- ### Exercise (3 stars): more_exercises (Optional) ⭐⭐⭐
413-
414--- Take a piece of paper. For each of the following theorems,
415--- first *think* about whether (a) it can be proved using only
416--- simplification and rewriting, (b) it also requires case
417--- analysis (`cases`), or (c) it also requires induction. Write
418--- down your prediction. Then fill in the proof. (There is no

315--- ### Falsehood and Negation
316-
317--- Up to this point, we have mostly been concerned with proving
318--- "positive" statements — addition is commutative, appending
319--- lists is associative, etc. We are sometimes also interested
320--- in negative results, demonstrating that some proposition is
321--- *not* true. Such statements are expressed with the logical
322--- negation operator `¬`, which is a prefix notation for `Not`.
323-
324--- To see how negation works, recall the *principle of
325--- explosion* from the `Tactics` chapter, which asserts that,
326--- if we assume a contradiction, then any other proposition can
327--- be derived.
328-
329--- Following this intuition, we could define `¬ a` ("not `a`")
330--- as `∀ c, a → c`. Lean makes an equivalent but slightly
331--- different choice, defining `¬ a` as `a → False`, where
332--- `False` is a specific unprovable proposition defined in the
333--- standard library.
311+--  ### Falsehood and Negation
312+
313+--  Up to this point, we have mostly been concerned with
314+--  proving "positive" statements — addition is commutative,
315+--  appending lists is associative, etc. We are sometimes
316+--  also interested in negative results, demonstrating that
317+--  some proposition is *not* true. Such statements are
318+--  expressed with the logical negation operator `¬`, which
319+--  is a prefix notation for `Not`.
320+
321+--  To see how negation works, recall the *principle of
322+--  explosion* from the `Tactics` chapter, which asserts
323+--  that, if we assume a contradiction, then any other
324+--  proposition can be derived.
325+
326+--  Following this intuition, we could define `¬ a` ("not
327+--  `a`") as `∀ c, a → c`. Lean makes an equivalent but
328+--  slightly different choice, defining `¬ a` as
329+--  `a → False`, where `False` is a specific unprovable
330+--  proposition defined in the standard library.

486+--  ### Logical Equivalence
487+
488+--  The handy "if and only if" connective, which asserts
489+--  that two propositions have the same truth value, is a
490+--  structure containing the two implication directions.
491+--  `a ↔ b` is notation for `Iff a b`.
492+
493+--  You can use `Iff.mp` to access the forward direction of
494+--  the iff, `Iff.mpr` to access the backwards direction,
495+--  and `Iff.intro` to convert a goal of the form `a ↔ b` to
496+--  two goals of the form `a → b` and `b → a`.

623+--  ## Programming with Propositions
624+
625+--  What does it mean to say that "an element `x` occurs in
626+--  a list `l`"?
627+
628+--  - If `l` is the empty list, then `x` cannot occur in it,
629+--    so the property "`x` appears in `l`" is simply false.
630+
631+--  - Otherwise, `l` has the form `[x' :: l']`. In this
632+--    case, `x` occurs in `l` if it is equal to `x'` or if
633+--    it occurs in `l'`.
634+
635+--  We can translate this directly into a straightforward
636+--  recursive function taking an element and a list and
637+--  returning... a proposition!
684638 
685639 def List.In {α : Type} (x : α) (xs : List α) : Prop :=
686640   match xs with
692646 
693647 theorem List.In_cons {α : Type} {x x' : α} {xs : List α} : List.In x (x' :: xs) = (x = x' ∨ List.In x xs) := rfl
694648

709663     In (f x) (map f xs) := by
716670     · rw [h, map_cons, In_cons]; left; rfl
717671     · rw [map_cons, In_cons]; right; exact ih h

693+--  Lean checks the *statements* of the `Nat.add_comm` and

699+--  Why?

701+--  The reason is that the identifier `Nat.add_comm`
702+--  actually refers to a *proof object* — a logical

704+--  `∀ n m : Nat, n + m = m + n`. The type of this object is

706+
707+--  The type of an ordinary function tells us what we can do
708+--  with it.
709+
710+--  - If we have a term of type `Nat → Nat → Nat`, we can
711+--    give it two `Nat`s as arguments and get a `Nat` back.
712+--    Similarly, the statement of a theorem tells us what we
713+--    can use that theorem for.
714+
715+--  - If we have a term of type
716+--    `∀ n m : Nat, n = m → n + n = m + m`, and we provide
717+--    it two numbers `n` and `m` and a third "argument" of
718+--    type `n = m`, we get back a proof object of type
719+--    `n + n = m + m`.
720+

912--- We've seen two different ways of expressing logical claims

914--- *propositions* (of type `Prop`). Here are the key
915--- differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
916-
917---   |                     | `Bool` | `Prop` |

920---   | useable with match? | yes    | no     |
921-
922--- Since functions in Lean by default must terminate on all
923--- inputs, a terminating function of type `Nat → Bool` is a
924--- *decision procedure* — i.e., it yields `true` or `false` on
925--- all inputs.
926-
927--- For example, `Nat.even` is a decision procedure for the
928--- property "is even".
929-
930--- Since `Prop` includes *both* decidable and undecidable
931--- properties, we have two options when we want to formalize a
932--- property that happens to be decidable: we can express it
933--- either as a boolean computation, or as a function into
934--- `Prop`.
935-
936--- For instance, to claim that a number `n` is even, we can say
937--- either that `Nat.even n` evaluates to `true`...
859+--  ## Working with Decidable Properties
860+
861+--  We've seen two different ways of expressing logical
862+--  claims in Lean: with *booleans* (of type `Bool`), and
863+--  with *propositions* (of type `Prop`). Here are the key
864+--  differences between `Bool` and `Prop`:
865+
866+--    |                     | `Bool` | `Prop` |
867+--    | ------------------- | ------ | ------ |
868+--    | decidable?          | yes    | no     |
869+--    | useable with match? | yes    | no     |
870+
871+--  Since functions in Lean by default must terminate on all

3--- # Preface
4-
5--- ## Welcome
6-
7--- This is the starting point for a series of electronic
8--- textbooks on *Software Foundations*, the mathematical
9--- underpinnings of reliable software. Topics in the series
10--- include basic concepts of logic, functional programming,
11--- computer-assisted theorem proving, operational semantics,
12--- logics and techniques for reasoning about programs, static
13--- type systems, property-based random testing, and
14--- verification of practical C code. The exposition is intended
15--- for a broad range of readers, from advanced undergraduates
16--- to PhD students and researchers. No specific background in
17--- logic or programming languages is assumed, though a degree
18--- of mathematical maturity will be helpful.
19-
20--- The principal novelty of the series is that it is one
21--- hundred percent formalized and machine-checked: each text is
22--- literally a script for Lean. The books are intended to be
23--- read alongside (or inside) an interactive session with Lean.
24--- All the details in the text are fully formalized in Lean,
25--- and almost all of the exercises are designed to be worked
26--- using Lean.
27-
28--- This book, *Logical Foundations in Lean*, lays groundwork
29--- for the others, introducing the reader to the basic ideas of
30--- functional programming, formal logic, and Lean itself.
31-
32--- ## Overview
33-
34--- Building reliable software is hard -- really hard. The scale
35--- and complexity of modern systems, the number of people
36--- involved, and the range of demands placed on them make it
37--- challenging to build software that is even more-or-less
38--- correct, much less 100% correct. At the same time, the
39--- increasing degree to which information processing is woven
40--- into every aspect of society greatly amplifies the cost of
41--- bugs and insecurities.
42-
43--- Computer scientists and software engineers have responded to
44--- these challenges with a host of techniques for improving
45--- software reliability, ranging from recommendations about
46--- managing software projects teams (e.g., extreme programming)
47--- to design philosophies for libraries (e.g.,
48--- model-view-controller, publish-subscribe, etc.) and whole
49--- programming languages (e.g., object-oriented programming,
50--- functional programming, ...) to mathematical techniques for
51--- specifying and reasoning about properties of software and
52--- tools for helping validate these properties. The *Software
53--- Foundations* books are focused on this last set of tools.
54-
55--- The present volume weaves together three conceptual threads:
56-
57--- - basic tools from *logic* for making and justifying precise
58---   claims about programs;
59-
60--- - the use of *provers* (or *proof assistants*) to construct
61---   rigorous logical arguments;
62-
63--- - *functional programming*, both as a programming method that
64---   simplifies reasoning about programs and as a bridge between
65---   programming and logic.
66-
67--- ### Logic
68-
69--- Logic is the field of study whose subject matter is *proofs*
70--- -- unassailable arguments for the truth of particular
71--- propositions. Volumes have been written about the central
72--- role of logic in computer science. called it "the calculus
73--- of computer science," while 's paper *On the Unusual
74--- Effectiveness of Logic in Computer Science* catalogs scores
75--- of ways in which logic offers critical tools and insights.
76--- Indeed, they observe that, "As a matter of fact, logic has
77--- turned out to be significantly more effective in computer
78--- science than it has been in mathematics. This is quite
79--- remarkable, especially since much of the impetus for the
80--- development of logic during the past one hundred years came
81--- from mathematics."
82-
83--- In particular, the fundamental tools of *inductive proof*
84--- are ubiquitous across computer science. You have surely seen
85--- them before, perhaps in a course on discrete math or
86--- analysis of algorithms, but in this book we will examine
87--- them more deeply than you have probably done so far.
88-
89--- ### Proof Assistants
90-
91--- The flow of ideas between logic and computer science over
92--- the years has run in both directions, with CS also making
93--- contributions to logic. One of these has been the
94--- development of software tools for helping construct and
95--- validate proofs of logical statements. These tools fall into
96--- two broad categories:
97-
98--- - *Automated theorem provers* provide "push-button" operation:
99---   you give them a proposition and they return either *true* or
100---   *false* (or, sometimes, *don't know: ran out of time*).
101---   Although their reasoning capabilities are limited, they have
102---   matured tremendously in recent decades and are used now in a
103---   multitude of settings. Examples of such tools include SAT
104---   solvers, SMT solvers, and model checkers.
105-
106--- - *Proof assistants* — or just *provers* — are hybrid tools
107---   that automate the more routine aspects of creating proofs
108---   while depending on human guidance for more difficult
109---   aspects. Widely used proof assistants include Isabelle,
110---   Agda, Twelf, ACL2, PVS, F*, HOL4, Rocq, and Lean, among many
111---   others.
112-
113--- This course is based around Lean, a proof assistant that has
114--- been under development since 2013 and has attracted a large
115--- and active community of users in both research and at
116--- companies like DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, MSR, and AWS.
117-
118--- Lean provides a rich environment for interactive development
119--- of machine-checked formal reasoning. The kernel of the Lean
120--- system is a simple proof-checker, which guarantees that only
121--- correct deduction steps are ever performed. On top of this
122--- kernel, the Lean environment provides high-level facilities
123--- for proof development, including a large library of common
124--- definitions and lemmas, powerful tactics for constructing
125--- complex proofs semi-automatically, and a highly extensible
126--- system for defining new proof-automation tactics and
127--- notations for specific situations.
128-
129--- Lean and its relatives have become critical enablers for a
130--- [huge variety of
131--- work](https://leanprover-community.github.io/papers.html)
132--- across computer science and mathematics:
133-
134--- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
135---     The individual references above should be merged into
136---     the categories below. In particular, the first three
137---     should go in the bullet about math, and the last one
138---     should go in the bullet about modeling programming
139---     languages. (I see that that first bullet could also use
140---     citations for some of the points it already makes, but
141---     we can leave that for later...)
142-
143--- - As a *platform for modeling programming languages*, proof
144---   assistants have become standard tools for researchers who
145---   need to describe and reason about complex language
146---   definitions. They have been used, for example, to check the
147---   security of the JavaCard platform, obtaining the highest
148---   level of common criteria certification, and for formal
149---   specifications of the x86 and LLVM instruction sets and
150---   programming languages such as C.
151-
152--- - As *environments for developing formally certified software
153---   and hardware*, they have been used, for example, to build
154---   CompCert, a fully-verified optimizing compiler for C,
155---   [Cedar](https://github.com/cedar-policy/cedar-spec), a
156---   formally-specified policy language, and CertiKOS, a fully
157---   verified hypervisor, for proving the correctness of subtle
158---   algorithms involving floating point numbers, and as the
159---   basis for CertiCrypt, FCF, and SSProve, which are frameworks
160---   for proving cryptographic algorithms secure. They are also
161---   being used to build verified implementations of the
162---   open-source RISC-V processor architecture.
163-
164--- - As *proof assistants for mathematics*, they have been used
165---   to validate and help develop a number of important results.
166---   For example, the ability to include complex computations
167---   inside proofs made it possible to develop the first formally
168---   verified proof of the 4-color theorem. This proof had
169---   previously been controversial among mathematicians because
170---   it required checking a large number of configurations using
171---   a program. More recently, an even more massive effort led to
172---   a formalization of the Feit-Thompson Theorem, the first
173---   major step in the classification of finite simple groups.
174---   Specifically, Lean is currently at the core of various
175---   formalization efforts in mathematics, such as the proof of
176---   [Fermat's Last
177---   Theorem](https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT), the
178---   [Sphere Packing
179---   Problem](https://github.com/thefundamentaltheor3m/Sphere-Packing-Lean).
180---   and even DeepMind's AI model for IMO problems
181---   [AlphaProof](https://deepmind.google/blog/ai-solves-imo-problems-at-silver-medal-level/).
182-
183--- ### Functional Programming
184-
185--- *Functional programming* refers both to a collection of
186--- idioms that can be used in almost any programming language
187--- and to a family of languages designed to foreground these
188--- idioms, including Haskell, OCaml, Standard ML, F#, Scala,
189--- Scheme, Racket, Common Lisp, Clojure, Erlang, F*, and Lean
190--- itself.
191-
192--- Functional programming has been developed over many decades
193--- — indeed, its roots go back to Church's lambda-calculus from
194--- the 1930s, well *before* the first electronic computers! But
195--- since the early '90s it has enjoyed a surge of interest
196--- among both software engineers and language designers.
197-
198--- The most basic tenet of functional programming is that,
199--- whenever possible, computation should be *pure*, in the
200--- sense that the only effect of execution should be to produce
201--- a result: it should be free from *side effects* such as I/O,
202--- assignments to mutable variables, redirecting pointers, etc.
203--- For example, whereas an *imperative* sorting function might
204--- take a list of numbers and rearrange its pointers to put the
205--- list in order, a pure sorting function would take the
206--- original list and return a fresh list containing the same
207--- numbers in sorted order.
208-
209--- A significant benefit of this style of programming is that
210--- it makes programs easier to understand and reason about. If
211--- every operation on a data structure yields a new data
212--- structure, leaving the old one intact, then there is no need
213--- to worry about how that structure is being shared and
214--- whether a change by one part of the program might break an
215--- invariant relied on by another part of the program. These
216--- considerations are particularly critical in concurrent
217--- systems, where every piece of mutable state shared between
218--- threads is a potential source of pernicious bugs.
219-
220--- Another reason for the popularity of functional programming
221--- is related to the first: functional programs are often much
222--- easier to parallelize and physically distribute than their
223--- imperative counterparts. If running a computation has no
224--- effect other than producing a result, then it does not
225--- matter *where* it is run. Similarly, if a data structure is
226--- never modified destructively, it can be copied freely,
227--- across cores or across the network. Indeed, the "Map-Reduce"
228--- idiom, which lies at the heart of massively distributed
229--- query processors like Hadoop and is used by Google to index
230--- the entire web, is a classic example of functional
231--- programming.
232-
233--- For purposes of these books, functional programming has yet
234--- another significant attraction: it serves as a bridge
235--- between logic and computer science. Indeed, Lean itself can
236--- be viewed as a combination of a small but extremely
237--- expressive functional programming language and a set of
238--- tools for stating and proving logical assertions. Moreover,
239--- when we come to look more closely, we find that these two
240--- sides of Lean are actually aspects of the very same
241--- underlying machinery -- i.e., *proofs are programs*.
242-
243--- ### Further Reading
244-
245--- This text is intended to be self contained, but readers
246--- looking for follow-on textbooks or deeper treatments of
247--- particular topics will find some suggestions for further
248--- reading in the Postscript chapter.
249-
250--- ## Practicalities
251-
252--- ### System Requirements
253-
254--- Lean runs on Windows, Linux, and MacOS. The files in this
255--- book have been tested with Lean version `4.33.0`.
256-
257--- ### Installation
258-
259--- The Visual Studio Code IDE is the recommended platform for
260--- using Lean.
261-
262--- - Install VS Code if needed
263-
264--- - From the Extensions tab of VS Code, install the Lean 4
265---   extension
266-
267--- - Clone the [SF-in-Lean](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean)
268---   git repo and open it in VS Code
269-
270--- - The first time you open a Lean file, the extension will
271---   offer to install Lean itself; accept, and it will fetch the
272---   version this book needs
273-
274--- - Wait for Lean to build the project (it takes a few minutes)
275-
276--- Note to developers (Claude @AI assistant, before next release):
277---     These steps send the reader to the **sources** repo, but
278---     the files a reader is meant to work in are the ones the
279---     build generates: `make lf-student` writes a standalone
280---     Lake project (its own `lakefile.toml` and
281---     `lean-toolchain`) to `_out/lf/student/lean`, and that is
282---     where the exercises with `sorry`s live. The `LF/*.lean`
283---     files in the repo are Verso documents — prose plus code
284---     blocks — and building the repo builds Verso and all
285---     three volumes, which is a good deal more than "a few
286---     minutes".
287---
288---     There is also a chicken-and-egg problem in the ordering:
289---     running `make` at all needs `elan`/`lake` already
290---     installed, but the step above gets Lean via the VS Code
291---     extension, which only offers it once a Lean project is
292---     open.
293---
294---     Both go away once there is a released archive of the
295---     student `.lean` files: the steps become "download and
296---     unpack, open the folder in VS Code, accept the install
297---     prompt". Until that exists, this section should probably
298---     say plainly that readers get the files from their
299---     instructor or by following `ALPHA-TESTERS.md`.

3+--  # Preface
4+
5+--  ## Welcome
6+
7+--  This is the starting point for a series of electronic
8+--  textbooks on *Software Foundations*, the mathematical
9+--  underpinnings of reliable software. Topics in the series
10+--  include basic concepts of logic, functional programming,
11+--  computer-assisted theorem proving, operational
12+--  semantics, logics and techniques for reasoning about
13+--  programs, static type systems, property-based random
14+--  testing, and verification of practical C code. The
15+--  exposition is intended for a broad range of readers,
16+--  from advanced undergraduates to PhD students and
17+--  researchers. No specific background in logic or
18+--  programming languages is assumed, though a degree of
19+--  mathematical maturity will be helpful.
20+
21+--  The principal novelty of the series is that it is one
22+--  hundred percent formalized and machine-checked: each
23+--  chapter of each book is literally a script for the Lean
24+--  prover, and the books are intended to be read alongside
25+--  (or inside) an interactive session with Lean. All the
26+--  details are fully formalized, and almost all of the
27+--  exercises are designed to be worked using Lean.
28+
29+--  This book, *Logical Foundations in Lean*, lays
30+--  groundwork for the others in the series, introducing the
31+--  reader to the basic ideas of functional programming,
32+--  formal logic, and Lean itself.
33+
34+--  ## Overview
35+
36+--  Building reliable software is hard -- really hard. The
37+--  scale and complexity of modern systems, the number of
38+--  people involved, and the range of demands placed on them
39+--  make it challenging to build software that is even
40+--  more-or-less correct, much less 100% correct. At the
41+--  same time, the increasing degree to which information
42+--  processing is woven into every aspect of society greatly
43+--  amplifies the cost of bugs and insecurities.
44+
45+--  Computer scientists and software engineers have
46+--  responded to these challenges with a host of techniques
47+--  for improving software reliability, ranging from
48+--  recommendations about managing software projects teams
49+--  (e.g., extreme programming) to design philosophies for
50+--  libraries (e.g., model-view-controller,
51+--  publish-subscribe, etc.) and whole programming languages
52+--  (e.g., object-oriented programming, functional
53+--  programming, ...) to mathematical techniques for
54+--  specifying and reasoning about properties of software
55+--  and tools for helping validate these properties. The
56+--  *Software Foundations* books are focused on this last
57+--  set of tools.
58+
59+--  The present volume weaves together three conceptual
60+--  threads:
61+
62+--  - basic tools from *logic* for making and justifying
63+--    precise claims about programs;
64+
65+--  - the use of *provers* (or *proof assistants*) to
66+--    construct rigorous logical arguments;
67+
68+--  - *functional programming*, both as a programming method
69+--    that simplifies reasoning about programs and as a
70+--    bridge between programming and logic.
71+
72+--  ### Logic
73+
74+--  Logic is the field of study whose subject matter is
75+--  *proofs* -- unassailable arguments for the truth of
76+--  particular propositions. Volumes have been written about
77+--  the central role of logic in computer science. Manna and
78+--  Waldinger (1971) called it "the calculus of computer
79+--  science," while Halpern *et al.* (2001)'s paper *On the
80+--  Unusual Effectiveness of Logic in Computer Science*
81+--  catalogs scores of ways in which logic offers critical
82+--  tools and insights. Indeed, they observe that, "As a
83+--  matter of fact, logic has turned out to be significantly
84+--  more effective in computer science than it has been in
85+--  mathematics. This is quite remarkable, especially since
86+--  much of the impetus for the development of logic during
87+--  the past one hundred years came from mathematics."
88+
89+--  In particular, the fundamental tools of *inductive
90+--  proof* are ubiquitous across computer science. You have
91+--  surely seen them before, perhaps in a course on discrete
92+--  math or analysis of algorithms, but in this book we will
93+--  examine them more deeply than you have probably done so
94+--  far.
95+
96+--  ### Proof Assistants
97+
98+--  The flow of ideas between logic and computer science
99+--  over the years has run in both directions, with CS also
100+--  making key contributions to logic. One of these has been
101+--  the development of software tools for helping construct
102+--  and validate proofs of logical statements. These tools
103+--  fall into two broad categories:
104+
105+--  - *Automated theorem provers* provide "push-button"
106+--    operation: you give them a proposition and they return
107+--    either *true* or *false* (or, sometimes, *don't know:
108+--    ran out of time*). Although their reasoning
109+--    capabilities are limited, they have matured
110+--    tremendously in recent decades and are used now in a
111+--    multitude of settings. Examples of such tools include
112+--    SAT solvers, SMT solvers, and model checkers.
113+
114+--  - *Proof assistants* — or just *provers* — are hybrid
115+--    tools that automate the more routine aspects of
116+--    creating proofs while depending on human guidance for
117+--    more difficult aspects. Widely used proof assistants
118+--    include Isabelle, Agda, Twelf, ACL2, PVS, F*, HOL4,
119+--    Rocq, and Lean, among many others.
120+
121+--  This course is based around Lean, a prover that has been
122+--  under development since 2013 and that has attracted a
123+--  large and active community of users in both research and
124+--  at companies like DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, MSR, and
125+--  AWS.
126+
127+--  Lean provides a rich environment for interactive
128+--  development of machine-checked formal reasoning. The
129+--  kernel of the Lean system is a simple proof-checker,
130+--  which guarantees that only correct deduction steps are
131+--  ever performed. On top of this kernel, the Lean
132+--  environment provides high-level facilities for proof
133+--  development, including a large library of common
134+--  definitions and lemmas, powerful tactics for
135+--  constructing complex proofs semi-automatically, and a
136+--  highly extensible system for defining new
137+--  proof-automation tactics and notations for specific
138+--  situations.
139+
140+--  Lean and its relatives have become critical enablers for
141+--  a [huge variety of
142+--  work](https://leanprover-community.github.io/papers.html)
143+--  across computer science and mathematics:
144+
145+--  - As a *platform for modeling programming languages*,
146+--    proof assistants have become standard tools for
147+--    researchers who need to describe and reason about
148+--    complex language definitions. They have been used, for
149+--    example, to check the security of the JavaCard
150+--    platform, obtaining the highest level of common
151+--    criteria certification, and for formal specifications
152+--    of the x86 and LLVM instruction sets and programming
153+--    languages such as C.
154+
155+--  - As *environments for developing formally certified
156+--    software and hardware*, they have been used, for
157+--    example, to build CompCert (Leroy *et al.*, 2016), a
158+--    fully-verified optimizing compiler for C,
159+--    [Cedar](https://github.com/cedar-policy/cedar-spec)
160+--    (Disselkoen *et al.*, 2024), a formally-specified
161+--    policy language, and CertiKOS (Gu *et al.*, 2016), a
162+--    fully verified hypervisor, and for proving the
163+--    correctness of subtle algorithms involving floating
164+--    point numbers, and as the basis for CertiCrypt, FCF,
165+--    and SSProve, which are frameworks for proving
166+--    cryptographic algorithms secure. They are also being
167+--    used to build verified implementations of the
168+--    open-source RISC-V processor architecture.
169+
170+--  - As *proof assistants for mathematics*, they have been
171+--    used to validate and help develop a number of
172+--    important results. For example, the ability to include
173+--    complex computations inside proofs made it possible to
174+--    develop the first formally verified proof of the
175+--    4-color theorem, which had previously been
176+--    controversial among mathematicians because the
177+--    argument required checking a large number of
178+--    configurations using a program. More recently, an even
179+--    more massive effort led to a formalization of the
180+--    Feit-Thompson Theorem, the first major step in the
181+--    classification of finite simple groups.
182+
183+--    Lean, in particular, is now at the core of various
184+--    formalization efforts in mathematics, such as the
185+--    proof of [Fermat's Last
186+--    Theorem](https://github.com/ImperialCollegeLondon/FLT),
187+--    the [Sphere Packing
188+--    Problem](https://github.com/thefundamentaltheor3m/Sphere-Packing-Lean).
189+--    and even DeepMind's AI model for International Math
190+--    Olympiad problems,
191+--    [AlphaProof](https://deepmind.google/blog/ai-solves-imo-problems-at-silver-medal-level/).
192+
193+--  ### Functional Programming
194+
195+--  *Functional programming* refers both to a collection of
196+--  powerful coding idioms that can be used in almost any
197+--  programming language and to a family of languages
198+--  designed to foreground these idioms, including Haskell,
199+--  OCaml, Standard ML, F#, Scala, Scheme, Racket, Common
200+--  Lisp, Clojure, Erlang, F*, and Lean itself.
201+
202+--  Functional programming has been developed over many
203+--  decades — indeed, its roots go back to Church's
204+--  lambda-calculus from the 1930s, well *before* the first
205+--  electronic computers! But since the early '90s it has
206+--  enjoyed a surge of interest among both software
207+--  engineers and language designers.
208+
209+--  The basic tenet of functional programming is that,
210+--  whenever possible, computation should be *pure*, in the
211+--  sense that the only effect of execution should be to
212+--  produce a result. That is, it should be free from *side
213+--  effects* such as I/O, assignments to mutable variables,
214+--  redirecting pointers, etc. For example, whereas an
215+--  *imperative* sorting function might take a list of
216+--  numbers and rearrange its pointers to put the list in
217+--  order, a pure sorting function would take the original
218+--  list and return a fresh list containing the same numbers
219+--  in sorted order.
220+
221+--  A significant benefit of this style of programming is
222+--  that it makes programs easier to understand and reason
223+--  about. If every operation on a data structure yields a
224+--  new data structure and leaves the old one intact, then
225+--  there is no need to worry about how that structure is
226+--  being shared and whether a change by one part of the
227+--  program might break an invariant relied on by another
228+--  part of the program. This is particularly important when
229+--  reasoning about concurrent systems, where every piece of
230+--  mutable state shared between threads is a potential
231+--  source of pernicious bugs.
232+
233+--  Another reason for the popularity of functional
234+--  programming, related to the first, is that functional
235+--  programs are often much easier to parallelize and
236+--  physically distribute than their imperative
237+--  counterparts. If running a computation has no effect
238+--  other than producing a result, then it does not matter
239+--  *where* it is run. Likewise, if a data structure is
240+--  never modified destructively, it can be copied freely,
241+--  across cores or across the network. Indeed, the
242+--  "Map-Reduce" idiom, which lies at the heart of massively
243+--  distributed query processors like Hadoop and is used by
244+--  Google to index the entire web, is a classic example of
245+--  functional programming.
246+
247+--  For these books, functional programming has yet another
248+--  significant attraction: it serves as a bridge between
249+--  logic and computer science. Indeed, Lean itself can be
250+--  viewed as a combination of a small but extremely
251+--  expressive functional programming language and a set of
252+--  tools for stating and proving logical assertions.
253+--  Moreover, when we come to look more closely, we find
254+--  that these two sides of Lean are actually aspects of the
255+--  very same underlying machinery -- i.e., *proofs are
256+--  programs*.
257+
258+--  ### Further Reading
259+
260+--  This text is intended to be self contained, but readers
261+--  looking for follow-on textbooks or deeper treatments of
262+--  particular topics will find some suggestions for further
263+--  reading in the Postscript chapter.
264+
265+--  ## Practicalities
266+
267+--  ### System Requirements
268+
269+--  Lean runs on Linux, MacOS, and Windows. The files in
270+--  this book have been tested with Lean version `4.33.0`.
271+
272+--  ### Installation
273+
274+--  The Visual Studio Code IDE is the recommended platform
275+--  for using Lean. To get set up, follow these steps:
276+
277+--  - Install VS Code if needed.
278+
279+--  - From the Extensions tab of VS Code, install the Lean 4
280+--    extension.
281+
282+--  - Clone the
283+--    [SF-in-Lean](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean) git
284+--    repo and open it in VS Code.
285+
286+--  - Open a Lean file; the extension will offer to install
287+--    Lean; accept, and it will fetch the version this book
288+--    needs.
289+
290+--  - Wait for Lean to build the project (it takes a few
291+--    minutes).
292+
293+--  ### Exercises
294+
295+--  Each chapter includes numerous exercises. Each is marked
296+--  with a "star rating," which can be interpreted as
297+--  follows:
298+
299+--  - One star: easy exercises that underscore points in the
300+--    text and that, for most readers, should take only a
301+--    minute or two. Get in the habit of working these as
302+--    you reach them.
303+
304+--  - Two stars: straightforward exercises (five or ten
305+--    minutes).
306+
307+--  - Three stars: exercises requiring a bit of thought (ten
308+--    minutes to half an hour).
309+
310+--  - Four and five stars: more difficult exercises (half an
311+--    hour and up).
312+
313+--  Those using SF in a classroom setting should note that
314+--  the autograder assigns extra points to harder exercises:
315+
316+--  1 star  = 1 point
317+--  2 stars = 2 points
318+--  3 stars = 3 points
319+--  4 stars = 6 points
320+--  5 stars = 10 points
321+
322+--  Some exercises are marked "advanced," and some are
323+--  marked "optional." Optional exercises provide a bit of
324+--  extra practice with key concepts and introduce secondary
325+--  themes that may be of interest to some readers. Advanced
326+--  exercises offer an extra challenge and a deeper cut at
327+--  the ideas. Doing just the non-optional, non-advanced
328+--  exercises should provide good coverage of the core
329+--  material.
330+

192+
193+--  The constructors of inductive types are *injective* (or

519-

522--- get us closer to the main goal we're trying to prove. Often,
523--- though, these facts are just special cases of more general
524--- hypotheses we already have.
525-
526--- If `h` is a quantified hypothesis in the current context —

529--- For example, `have h := h e` introduces a new `h` which `x`

531-
532--- For example:
496+--  ## Specializing Hypotheses
497+
498+--  We've already seen how we can use `have` to do forward
499+--  reasoning, by letting us state and prove useful facts
500+--  that get us closer to the main goal we're trying to
501+--  prove. Often, though, these facts are just special cases
502+--  of more general hypotheses we already have.
503+
504+--  If `h` is a quantified hypothesis in the current context
505+--  — i.e., `h : ∀ (x : α), P x` — then we can use `have` to
506+--  obtain a special case of `h` by supplying a value for
507+--  `x`. For example, `have h := h e` introduces a new `h`
508+--  which `x` has been instantiated with `e`.
509+
510+--  For example:
533511 
534512 example (m : Nat) (h : ∀ n, m * n = 0) : m = 0 := by
535513   have h := h 1
536514   rw [Nat.mul_one] at h
537515   exact h
538516 
539--- You may notice that, in the above proof, the original `h` is
540--- still present in the context, although it is shadowed by the
541--- new `h`. Often we don't care to keep this old hypothesis
542--- around, and so we can use the `replace` tactic instead. It
543--- behaves like `have`, except that it gets rid of the old
544--- hypothesis afterwards when possible:
517+--  You may notice that, in the above proof, the original
518+--  `h` is still present in the context, although it is
519+--  shadowed by the new `h`. Often we don't care to keep
520+--  this old hypothesis around, and so we can use the
521+--  `replace` tactic instead. It behaves like `have`, except
522+--  that it gets rid of the old hypothesis afterwards when
523+--  possible:
545524 
546525 example (m : Nat) (h : ∀ n, m * n = 0) : m = 0 := by
547526   replace h := h 1
548527   rw [Nat.mul_one] at h
549528   exact h
550529 
551--- Specializing a hypothesis in this way is common enough that
552--- Lean provides the `specialize` tactic for it. For example,
553--- `specialize h 1` is a more concise way of writing
554--- `replace h := h 1`:
530+--  Specializing a hypothesis in this way is common enough
531+--  that Lean provides the `specialize` tactic for it. For
532+--  example, `specialize h 1` is a more concise way of
533+--  writing `replace h := h 1`:
555534 
556535 example (m : Nat) (h : ∀ n, m * n = 0) : m = 0 := by
557536   specialize h 1
558537   rw [Nat.mul_one] at h
559538   exact h

645627 theorem double_injective (n m : Nat) (h : n.double = m.double) : n = m := by
646628   induction n generalizing m with
657639       rw [Nat.double_succ, Nat.double_succ] at h
658640       injections
659641 
660--- The thing to take away from all this is that you need to be
661--- careful, when using induction, that your induction
662--- hypothesis is not too specific. When proving a proposition
663--- quantified over variables `n` and `m` by induction on `n`,
664--- it is sometimes crucial to *generalize* `m`, so that the
665--- induction hypothesis applies to every `m` rather than just
666--- the particular `m` in the context.

915895 theorem anyTrue_eq_anyTrue (α : Type) (test : α → Bool) (l : List α) :
916896     anyTrue test l = anyTrue' test l := by

82--- Typeclasses automate this — instead of the programmer
83--- passing the function explicitly, Lean searches for one and
84--- provides it on its own. We specify something we want Lean to
85--- search for by declaring a `class` with the needed function

88--- called *instance*; each type can have its own instance of a
89--- class. For functions that would use such instances, we
90--- specify the name of the class in a *instance implicit* on
91--- the polymorphic variable that the instance's function
92--- applies to. This directs Lean to rely on the class inside
93--- the function, and to find and fill in the appropriate
94--- instance when the function is called.

361--- ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
362-
363--- The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an
364--- instance may carry — any value of the right type will do.
365--- But sometimes enforcing constraints on data is useful. For
366--- example, suppose we want to specify that a type has not just
367--- a single element, but two. Here is a first attempt:
351+--  ## Proof-Carrying Typeclasses
352+
353+--  The above examples enforce no conditions on the data an
354+--  instance may carry — any value of the right type will
355+--  do. But sometimes enforcing constraints on data is
356+--  useful. For example, suppose we want to specify that a
357+--  type has not just a single element, but two. Here is a
358+--  first attempt:
368359 
369360 sf_experiment
370361   class HasTwoIncomplete (α : Type) where
371362     one : α
372363     two : α
373364 
374--- Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because it
375--- allows `one` and `two` to refer to the same term.
376--- Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses can carry proofs along with
377--- data, so we can write the following to enforce that `one`
378--- and `two` are distinct.
365+--  Unfortunately, this specification isn't precise because
366+--  it allows `one` and `two` to refer to the same term.
367+--  Fortunately, Lean's typeclasses can carry proofs along
368+--  with data, so we can write the following to enforce that
369+--  `one` and `two` are distinct.
379370 
380371 class HasTwo (α : Type) where
381372   one : α
382373   two : α
383374   one_neq_two : one ≠ two
384375 
385--- Declaring instances works in much the same way as before,
386--- except that now the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field requires a
387--- proof:
376+--  Declaring instances works in much the same way as
377+--  before, except that now the `HasTwo.one_neq_two` field
378+--  requires a proof:
388379 
389380 instance : HasTwo Nat where
390381   one := 1
391382   two := 2
392383   one_neq_two := by intro contra; contradiction

421--- This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively in
422--- Lean to define mathematical structures that carry both
423--- operators and laws about how those operators interact. As a
424--- simple example, let's use a typeclass to define a *monoid*,
425--- a simple algebraic structure that includes four things:
426-
427--- - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
428-
429--- - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that
430---   combines two elements of type `α` into one,
431-
432--- - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call the
433---   "identity element", and
434-
435--- - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`, namely
436---   that:
437-
438---   - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
439-
440---   - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗` is
441---     associative)
442-
443--- We can express these requirements in the form of a
444--- typeclass:
414+--  This facility is very powerful, and is used extensively
415+--  in Lean to define mathematical structures that carry
416+--  both operators and laws about how those operators
417+--  interact. As a simple example, let's use a typeclass to
418+--  define a *monoid*, a simple algebraic structure that
419+--  includes four things:
420+
421+--  - an underlying set of data, represented by a type `α`,
422+
423+--  - an operator (which we'll write `⊗`, typed otimes) that
424+--    combines two elements of type `α` into one,
425+
426+--  - a particular element `id` of type `α`, which we call
427+--    the "identity element", and
428+
429+--  - some laws about the interaction of `⊗` and `id`,
430+--    namely that:
431+
432+--    - `∀ x, id ⊗ x = x = x ⊗ id`, and
433+
434+--    - `∀ x y z, x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z` (i.e., that `⊗`
435+--      is associative)
436+
437+--  We can express these requirements in the form of a
438+--  typeclass:
445439 
446440 -- first we define a notation typeclass for our operator ⊗
447441 class OpSet (α : Type) where
455449   right_id : ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ id = x
456450   assoc : ∀ (x y z : α), x ⊗ (y ⊗ z) = (x ⊗ y) ⊗ z
457451

461--- "inherits" the fields of `OpSet`, similar to how a class
462--- would in an object-oriented language.

501--- In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can also
502--- prove some properties about monoids in general, just based
503--- on the laws defined on the typeclass. One simple theorem
504--- about monoids is that the identity element of a monoid is
505--- unique. That is, if we have two monoids over the same set
506--- with the same operator, their identity elements must also be
507--- the same:
498+--  In addition to defining instances of `Monoid`, we can
499+--  also prove some properties about monoids in general,
500+--  just based on the laws defined on the typeclass. One
501+--  simple theorem about monoids is that the identity
502+--  element of a monoid is unique. That is, if we have two
503+--  monoids over the same set with the same operator, their
504+--  identity elements must also be the same:
508505 
509506 theorem id_unique {α : Type} {m₁ m₂ : Monoid α} (h : m₁.op = m₂.op) : m₁.id = m₂.id := by
510507   obtain @⟨op₁, id₁, left_id₁, right_id₁, assoc₁⟩ := m₁
519516   -- the goal `m₁.id = m₂.id` is equivalent with `id₁ = id₂` even though it displays `Monoid.id = Monoid.id`
520517   exact h'
521518

526--- with the `@` symbol. When stepping through the above proof,

532--- are implicit arguments to `Monoid.id`. Setting
533--- `pp.explicit true` displays the goal as
534--- `@Eq α (@Monoid.id α m₁) (@Monoid.id α m₂)`.

533+--  A *group* is a special kind of monoid with an *inverse*
534+--  operation `inv`, which has the property that
535+--  `∀ x, inv x ⊗ x = id = x ⊗ inv x`. We can extend the
536+--  definition of a `Monoid` to capture this new feature:

541538 class Group (α : Type) extends (Monoid α) where
542539   inv : α → α
543540   left_inv : ∀ (x : α), inv x ⊗ x = id
544541   right_inv: ∀ (x : α), x ⊗ inv x = id

574+--  ## Maps
575+
576+--  *Maps* (or "dictionaries") are ubiquitous data
577+--  structures both in ordinary programming and in the
578+--  theory of programming languages; we're going to need
579+--  them in many places in later volumes.

582+--  include a "default" element to be returned when a key
583+--  being looked up doesn't exist, and *partial maps*, which
584+--  instead return an option to indicate success or failure.
585+--  Partial maps are defined in terms of total maps, using
586+--  `none` as the default element.

633--- The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction,

638--- of maps, as we saw with functions in the Logic chapter: two
639--- maps that respond to every query in the same way will be

641--- as "equivalent" list structures. This simplifies proofs that
642--- use maps.

622+--  ### Total Maps

624+--  The Lists chapter introduced a partial map abstraction,
625+--  `PartialMap`, with a `find` function for lookup, based
626+--  on lists of key-value pairs. Here, we are going to build
627+--  a map abstraction using functions instead. The advantage
628+--  of this representation is that it offers a more
629+--  *extensional* view of maps, as we saw with functions in
630+--  the Logic chapter: two maps that respond to every query
631+--  in the same way will be represented as exactly the same
632+--  function, rather than just as "equivalent" list
633+--  structures. This simplifies proofs that use maps.

635+--  Instead of using functions directly, we encapsulate them

1343+--  The crucial difference between the two worlds is
1344+--  decidability. Every (closed) Lean expression of type
1345+--  `Bool` can be simplified in a finite number of steps to
1346+--  either `true` or `false` — i.e., there is a terminating
1347+--  mechanical procedure for deciding whether or not it is
1348+--  true.
1349+
1350+--  This means that, for example, the type `Nat → Bool` is
1351+--  inhabited only by functions that, given a `Nat`, always
1352+--  yield either `true` or `false` in finite time; and this,
1353+--  in turn, means (by a standard computability argument)
1354+--  that there is no function in `Nat → Bool` that checks
1355+--  whether a given number is the code of a terminating
1356+--  Turing machine.
1357+
1358+--  By contrast, the type `Prop` includes both decidable and
1359+--  undecidable mathematical propositions; in particular,
1360+--  the type `Nat → Prop` does contain functions
1361+--  representing properties like "the nth Turing machine
1362+--  halts." The second row in the table follows directly
1363+--  from this essential difference. To evaluate a pattern
1364+--  match (or conditional) on a boolean, we need to know
1365+--  whether the scrutinee evaluates to `true` or `false`;
1366+--  this only works for `Bool`, not `Prop`.
1367+
1368+--  The third row highlights an important practical
1369+--  difference: equality functions like `Nat.beq` that
1370+--  return a boolean cannot be used directly to justify
1371+--  rewriting with the rewrite tactic; propositional
1372+--  equality is required for this. Since `Prop` includes
1373+--  both decidable and undecidable properties, we have two
1374+--  options when we want to formalize a property that
1375+--  happens to be decidable: we can express it either as a
1376+--  boolean computation or as a function into Prop.

6--- # UsingLean: Using the Full Power of a Proof Assistant
7-
8--- In this chapter, we will learn to write more idiomatic Lean
9--- using its more powerful tools. This includes the natural
10--- numbers from its standard library, tactics which can search

7+
8+--  In this chapter, we will learn to write more idiomatic
9+--  Lean using its more powerful tools. This includes the
10+--  natural numbers from its standard library, tactics which
11+--  can search for lemmas from the standard library,
12+--  namespaces for organizing lemmas, and two new tactics,
13+--  `calc` and `dsimp`, which enable more readable and
14+--  concise proofs.

163---   = (m + n) + k        ...   [by commutativity of addition]
164---   = m + (n + k)        ...   [by associativity of addition]

146+--  ## Structuring Proofs with `calc`
147+
148+--  In Lean proofs, long `rw` chains are useful, but they
149+--  are sometimes hard to read because the intermediate
150+--  goals are invisible. Furthermore, sometimes we *know*
151+--  exactly how we want to manipulate the terms of a proof,
152+--  but don't want to have the tactics like `Nat.add_comm`
153+--  and `Nat.add_assoc` "guess" which subterms to rewrite.
154+
155+--  The `calc` tactic writes down the intermediate goals of
156+--  a proof, and allows us to specify exactly which rewrite
157+--  rules to apply at each step. It is designed to mimic the
158+--  style of proofs in mathematics textbooks, which will
159+--  often look something like this:
160+
161+--    n + (m + k)
162+--    = (n + m) + k        ...   [by associativity of addition]
163+--    = (m + n) + k        ...   [by commutativity of addition]
164+--    = m + (n + k)        ...   [by associativity of addition]
165+
166+--  Note how we can see each intermediate step of this proof
167+--  when we look at it this way. Let's look at how we might
168+--  prove this theorem (i.e., that
169+--  `n + (m + k) = m + (n + k)`) in Lean.
170+
171+--  First, a proof in the style we already know.
172172 
173173 example (n m k : Nat) : n + (m + k) = m + (n + k) := by
174174   rw [← Nat.add_assoc, Nat.add_comm n m, Nat.add_assoc]
175175 
176--- Here we present the same theorem, written with `calc`. Note
177--- how each intermediate goal is visible in the source.
176+--  Here we present the same theorem, written with `calc`.
177+--  Note how each intermediate goal is visible in the
178+--  source.
178179 
179180 example (n m k : Nat) : n + (m + k) = m + (n + k) := by
180181   calc n + (m + k) /- one side of the goal is the argument to `calc`...
185186        (in this case `m + (n + k)`), the calc tactic succeeds. -/
186187     (m + n) + k = m + (n + k) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
187188 
188--- We can also write the proof like this to be a bit more
189--- concise:
189+--  We can also write the proof like this to be a bit more
190+--  concise:
190191 
191192 example (n m k : Nat) : n + (m + k) = m + (n + k) := by
192193   calc n + (m + k)
194195     _ = (m + n) + k := by rw [Nat.add_comm n m]
195196     _ = m + (n + k) := by rw [Nat.add_assoc]
196197

198--- `calc` tactic was repeated from the right-hand side of the
199--- previous one, we can replace the left-hand side entirely
200--- with an `_`. Now our Lean proof looks quite a bit like the
201--- textbook one we saw earlier!

219--- ## Definitional Simplification: `dsimp`
220-
221--- Often, rather than repeatedly rewriting by a known equation
222--- like `rw [Nat.mul_zero, Nat.mul_zero]` to solve a goal like
223--- `n * (m * 0) = 0`, we just want to simplify the function
224--- (here `Nat.mul`) automatically when we can.
225-
226--- The `dsimp` ("definitionally simplify") tactic unfolds
227--- definitions and performs definitional simplifications. You
228--- can give it hints in square brackets: `dsimp [f]` tells it
229--- to unfold the definition of `f`. You can also simplify a
230--- hypothesis `h` in the context by writing `dsimp [...] at h`.
231--- `dsimp` will also close goals by `rfl` when possible.
216+--  If you prefer `rw` to `calc`, that's fine! Each has
217+--  particular uses, and both will be tools in your
218+--  ever-growing toolbox of tactics.

220+--  ## Definitional Simplification: `dsimp`
221+
222+--  Often, rather than repeatedly rewriting by a known
223+--  equation like `rw [Nat.mul_zero, Nat.mul_zero]` to solve
224+--  a goal like `n * (m * 0) = 0`, we just want to simplify
225+--  the function (here `Nat.mul`) automatically when we can.
226+
227+--  The `dsimp` ("definitionally simplify") tactic unfolds
228+--  definitions and performs definitional simplifications.
229+--  You can give it hints in square brackets: `dsimp [f]`
230+--  tells it to unfold the definition of `f`. You can also
231+--  simplify a hypothesis `h` in the context by writing
232+--  `dsimp [...] at h`. `dsimp` will also close goals by
233+--  `rfl` when possible.
232234 
233235 def square (n : Nat) : Nat := n * n
234236 
235237 def triple (n : Nat) : Nat := n + n + n
236238 
237--- When the goal depends on a fact about an unknown value,
238--- `rfl` fails. Here, `dsimp` makes progress, exposing a goal
239--- the fact can close.
239+--  When the goal depends on a fact about an unknown value,
240+--  `rfl` fails. Here, `dsimp` makes progress, exposing a
241+--  goal the fact can close.
240242 
241243 example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
242244   -- rfl will not work here!
244246   -- The goal can now be rewritten by `h`.
245247   rw [h]
246248 
247--- As we have seen, `rw` can also unfold definitions. In this
248--- example, either style is fine: use `dsimp [triple]` when you
249--- want to emphasize definitional simplification, or
250--- `rw [triple, h]` when the proof is just a sequence of
251--- rewrites.
249+--  As we have seen, `rw` can also unfold definitions. In
250+--  this example, either style is fine: use `dsimp [triple]`
251+--  when you want to emphasize definitional simplification,
252+--  or `rw [triple, h]` when the proof is just a sequence of
253+--  rewrites.
252254 
253255 example (n m : Nat) (h : n + n = m) : triple n = m + n := by
254256   -- `rw [triple]` unfolds `triple n`.
255257   rw [triple, h]
